# Twelve gaps: what is assumed and what is proved {#sec-critique}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Learning goals"}
- Know the three standard objections to the imaginary-coupling theories.
- Know the twelve gaps between what the literature uses and what it establishes.
- Know which chapter of Part VII (or Parts V and VI) addresses each gap, and with what status.
:::

Part VII asks whether the imaginary-coupling affine Toda theories exist as quantum field theories, in the operational sense of @sec-valid-qft. This chapter states the problem: the objections usually raised, the twelve specific gaps in the literature, and a summary of what the rest of the part establishes.

## Three objections {#sec-three-objections}

Three objections are routinely raised against the imaginary-coupling theories.

1. **Complex action.** For real fields the Euclidean weight $e^{-S_E}$ is complex, so it is unclear what measure is being integrated and whether the theory has a sign problem.
2. **Complex saddles.** The solitons are complex solutions of the field equations. A path integral over real fields gives no obvious reason to include them, and no criterion for which ones to include [@mackay_watts1995].
3. **Non-unitarity.** The Hamiltonian is not Hermitian and the S-matrices are not unitary. In some sectors the finite-volume spectrum is complex [@tw1999; @tw2002].

## The gaps {#sec-gaps}

We list the gaps between what the literature uses and what it establishes. In each case we state precisely what is missing.

**H1. Existence of the regularized theory.** For imaginary coupling the Euclidean weight $e^{-S_E}$ is complex. No paper we know of shows that a regularized imaginary-coupling ATFT defines finite, well-defined correlation functions, still less a probability-like measure.

**H2. Sign problem.** A complex weight usually means cancellations between configurations. If those cancellations were severe, the theory would be ill-defined in practice even on a lattice, and expectation values could be dominated by numerical noise.

**H3. Continuum limit.** The interaction is a sum of complex vertex operators. One must ask in which range of $\beta$ Wick ordering suffices, and whether the infinite-volume limit exists and has a mass gap. For real coupling, Albeverio–Høegh-Krohn methods apply. For imaginary coupling there is no analogous result.

**H4. Hilbert space.** The Hamiltonian is not Hermitian in the Schrödinger representation. The literature uses "non-unitary" without specifying an inner product, an adjoint, or the structure that replaces Hermiticity.

**H5. Vacuum.** With a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, nothing a priori guarantees a real ground-state energy, or even that the vacuum is the state of lowest real energy.

**H6. Classical reality.** Reality of soliton energies has been shown for specific solution classes. There are also complex-energy and negative-energy solutions [@khastgir1996], and singular ones. No general criterion distinguishes the solutions that should count as physical.

**H7. Complex saddles.** DHN semiclassics expands around complex solitons. The justification usually offered (steepest descent may leave the real contour) does not say *which* complex saddles contribute, nor with what weight [@mackay_watts1995].

**H8. Semiclassical quantization.** The fluctuation operator around a complex soliton is not Hermitian. Mode sums with orthonormal eigenfunctions assume it is diagonalizable, and independent calculations disagree ($c_n^{(1)}$ [@delius_grisaru1995; @mackay_watts1995]; $b_n^{(1)}$ semiclassics versus exact [@gmw1996]).

**H9. Non-unitarity.** Most soliton S-matrices are not unitary. Some amplitudes do not have phase eigenvalues, and finite-volume spectra can be complex [@tw1999; @tw2002]. It is unclear what replaces unitarity and what consistency conditions survive.

**H10. Exact S-matrices.** They are conjectures, built on quantum-group symmetry, R-matrix unitarity, crossing and the bootstrap. They were missing for four families; @sec-sm-introduction supplies three of them ($c_n^{(1)}$, $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$, $e_6^{(2)}$), and $f_4^{(1)}$ remains open (@sec-imaginary-coupling-quantum-theory). Even where they exist, identifying the full spectrum is subtle: a closed bootstrap can contain particles that are neither solitons nor breathers [@tw1999].

**H11. Missing classical solutions.** The topological charges of classical solitons do not fill the quantum multiplets [@mcghee1994]. Classical counterparts of some quantum bound states are not known [@tw1999].

**H12. Unitary subtheories.** RSOS restriction sometimes yields unitary theories and sometimes not, depending on the coupling, the gradation, and whether breathers survive. There is no general criterion.

## What Part VII establishes {#sec-summary-overview}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Abstract"}
Affine Toda field theories (ATFTs) are a family of two-dimensional integrable quantum field theories, one for each affine Kac–Moody algebra $\hat g$. With real coupling they are unitary theories of $\operatorname{rank}(g)$ scalar particles. Their exact S-matrices are known for every $\hat g$ and have been checked perturbatively and numerically.

With imaginary coupling they have a complex action, solitons that are complex classical saddles, and S-matrices that are generally not unitary. These features have long been taken to cast doubt on whether the imaginary-coupling theories exist as quantum field theories at all.

We review the field and list twelve gaps between what is used in practice and what has been established. We then build a foundation that closes as many as possible. Our results are:

- **Positivity.** On a lattice, every imaginary-coupling ATFT is a well-defined statistical model. After integrating out the free field, its partition function is a convergent sum of *positive* Coulomb-gas weights. The "complex action" therefore never produces a sign problem.
- **Krein structure.** The lattice transfer matrix is self-adjoint with respect to an indefinite (Krein) inner product whose fundamental symmetry is field parity $\vec\phi\mapsto-\vec\phi$. It commutes with an antilinear PT-type symmetry $\Theta$. So the spectrum is closed under complex conjugation.
- **Real vacuum energy.** Positivity of $\operatorname{Tr}T^N$ together with Pringsheim's theorem proves that the finite-volume vacuum energy is real and has the smallest real part in the spectrum. Excited levels can be complex, and an exactly solvable reduction shows they are.
- **Continuum limit.** In finite volume, with Wick ordering done site by site, the lattice theory has a continuum limit for every algebra and every coupling below the first collapse threshold, $\beta^2<\beta^2_{\rm UV}$. Every term of the Coulomb-gas expansion is positive (Theorems [-@thm-below-2pi] and [-@thm-window]). Without further counterterms the limit fails at and above $\beta^2_{\rm UV}$, and with site-independent Wick ordering it already fails at $2\pi$. Below $2\pi$ a nearest-neighbour bound suffices. In the window $2\pi\le\beta^2<\beta^2_{\rm UV}$ the proof keeps the exact interactions inside small clusters of charges, repulsion included, and uses a cluster bound on products of $m$-th-neighbour distances (Theorems [-@thm-nn-distances] and [-@thm-cluster-bound]). The resulting estimate is a stability bound on the free energy at real fugacity, with the exponent set by the bulk free energy (@lem-stability).
- **Classical reality.** Classical energies are real precisely for $\Theta$-invariant asymptotic data, which turns the old ad hoc restriction to "good" solutions into a symmetry statement.
- **Semiclassics.** The Picard–Lefschetz form of the semiclassical expansion requires eigenvalues to be counted with algebraic multiplicity. This resolves the long-standing disagreements over one-loop soliton masses. We derive the counting rule from the transmission factors. Jordan blocks have the sizes of their zeros (@thm-jordan-chains), and the multiplicity of an isolated eigenvalue is the net order of the product of all transmission factors whenever the fluctuations have Hirota form (@thm-hirota-factorization). A zero in one channel can be cancelled by a pole in another, and weight can be carried by a bounded threshold resonance rather than an $L^2$ vector (Propositions [-@prp-an-zeros] and [-@prp-cn-threshold-blocks]). The Hirota form holds for every static soliton of $d_n^{(1)}$ and $e_n^{(1)}$ and for their foldings, given a degree bound verified up to rank 8 (@prp-hirota-form). The resulting one-loop masses of all folded solitons agree with every known result, settle the $b_n^{(1)}$ disagreement, and predict the $f_4^{(1)}$ soliton masses (@sec-one-loop-masses-folded).
- **Scattering.** Braiding (R-matrix) unitarity, crossing and the bootstrap follow from the universal R-matrix [@delius1995], but they are not QFT unitarity, which in addition requires Hermitian analyticity [@miramontes1999]. What the Krein structure does imply is that eigenvalues of S-matrices and multi-particle transfer matrices are pure phases or come in pairs $(s,1/\bar s)$. This turns the Takács–Watts criterion for a real finite-volume spectrum into a criterion for unbroken $\Theta$. For the exact S-matrix of the fundamental solitons of $a_n^{(1)}$ the Krein structure is proved directly from the R-matrix, without asymptotic completeness (@prp-krein-fundamental). It confirms the observation of Takács and Watts that three-soliton states of $a_2^{(1)}$ are $\Theta$-broken, although the fundamental soliton–soliton amplitude has phase eigenvalues, and shows that the breaking is confined to states carrying all three colours. RSOS restriction to the perturbed $W_3(p,p')$ models makes the kink S-matrix Hermitian analytic and unitary exactly when $p'\equiv\pm1\pmod p$ (@prp-rsos-kinks). For $p'=p+2$ the kink sectors are also unbroken, yet no Hermitian-analytic basis exists.
- **What cannot be rescued.** We list the physical consequences of unitarity that fail in the unrestricted imaginary-coupling theories of rank $r\ge2$ and that no choice of inner product, basis, gradation or quantum-group restriction can restore, because their failure is detected by basis-independent quantities (@sec-unitarity).

The resulting picture is that imaginary-coupling ATFTs are valid **non-unitary** quantum field theories, in the same sense as the scaling Lee–Yang model. They have a positive Euclidean measure, a Krein-space Hamiltonian formulation, a real vacuum energy, real masses for the asymptotic particles in every known exact solution, and a consistent S-matrix theory. Unitarity is not one of their properties: it fails in identifiable sectors, and requiring it was a category error. @sec-unitarity states exactly which of its usual consequences are lost and cannot be recovered. We also correct a premise common in the literature: exact soliton S-matrices were *not* known for every algebra. They were missing for $c_n^{(1)}$ with $n\ge3$, $f_4^{(1)}$, $e_6^{(2)}$ and $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$. @sec-sm-introduction constructs them for $c_n^{(1)}$, $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ and $e_6^{(2)}$ (the first and second for the spinor soliton, verified for small $n$). For $f_4^{(1)}$ it constructs a candidate amplitude that satisfies all the axioms but is ruled out by a one-loop computation, so that case remains open.
:::

## Summary of results {#sec-summary-results}

| Gap | Content | Status |
|---|---|---|
| H1 | existence of the regularized theory | closed: Theorems [-@thm-bounded-weight] and [-@thm-coulomb-gas] (lattice) |
| H2 | sign problem from the complex action | closed: @thm-coulomb-gas (positive Coulomb gas) |
| H3 | continuum limit | proved here (awaiting independent check) in finite volume for $\beta^2<\beta^2_{\rm UV}$: @thm-below-2pi for $\beta^2<2\pi$, @thm-window in the window $2\pi\le\beta^2<\beta^2_{\rm UV}$; further counterterms needed at and above $\beta^2_{\rm UV}$ (@prp-uv-divergence); infinite volume open (@cnj-correlation-range) |
| H4 | Hilbert space and Hamiltonian | closed: @thm-krein-transfer (Krein space, $\Theta$-symmetry) |
| H5 | reality of the vacuum energy | closed: @thm-vacuum-energy |
| H6 | reality of classical energies; singular and complex-energy solutions | closed: @prp-hirota-energy and the $\Theta$ selection rule |
| H7 | which complex saddles contribute | reduced: thimble formulation; masses shown independent of the choice; intersection numbers computed and validated in a reduced model (@sec-which-saddles-contribute) |
| H8 | semiclassical mass corrections | closed: algebraic-multiplicity rule, with lattice and exact checks; counting rule derived from the transmission factors (Theorems [-@thm-jordan-chains] and [-@thm-hirota-factorization], @prp-net-count) and checked for $a_n^{(1)}$ and $c_n^{(1)}$ (Propositions [-@prp-an-zeros] and [-@prp-cn-threshold-blocks]); Hirota form for $d_n^{(1)}$, $e_n^{(1)}$ and their foldings given a degree bound verified to rank 8 (@prp-hirota-form); one-loop masses of all folded solitons, agreeing with every known exact result (@sec-one-loop-masses-folded) |
| H9 | non-unitarity of S-matrices and complex finite-volume spectra | reclassified: Krein-unitarity (@prp-krein-unitarity), exact on an integrable lattice regularization (@prp-krein-regularization) and for the exact fundamental-soliton S-matrices of $a_n^{(1)}$ (@prp-krein-fundamental); sector-by-sector classification; consequences of unitarity that cannot be rescued identified (@sec-unitarity) |
| H10 | completeness and correctness of exact S-matrices | partly open: soliton S-matrices constructed in Part VI for $c_n^{(1)}$, $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ and $e_6^{(2)}$, all three agreeing with the one-loop soliton masses (@sec-one-loop-masses-folded), and $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ also with integrable-lattice masses (@sec-a2n-lattice); $f_4^{(1)}$ open, with its one-loop soliton masses predicted (@sec-one-loop-masses-folded) |
| H11 | missing classical topological charges and solutions | open; reformulated via thimbles; static saddles shown not to suffice for $a_3^{(1)}$, whose missing charges are carried by charged two-soliton bound states (@sec-which-saddles-contribute) |
| H12 | unitary subtheories and RSOS restriction | established in specific cases; exact criterion for the fundamental kinks of $a_2^{(1)}$ (@prp-rsos-kinks); general criterion conjectured (@cnj-unitary-rsos) |

## Notes and references {#sec-critique-notes}

The objections are standard; see MacKay and Watts [-@mackay_watts1995] for the semiclassical ones and Takács and Watts [-@tw1999; -@tw2002] for non-unitarity. The list of gaps and the operational criteria are new here.
